title: The past tense
objectives: I can say what I did yesterday and last weekend, choosing the past form by the gender and number of the subject.
I can form the past of a regular verb from its infinitive, and use the special pasts of 'бу́ти', 'іти́', 'могти́', 'ї́сти' and 'нести́'.
I can say what someone had, what they did not have and who was not there, with 'був', 'була́', 'було́', 'були́' and 'не було́'.
I can ask and answer questions about past events, and say when they happened with 'вчо́ра', 'позавчо́ра', 'мину́лого ти́жня' and 'рік тому́'.
I can explain why the 'в' of 'чита́в' is said [w], and why the past of 'іти́' is 'ішо́в' after a consonant and 'йшов' after a vowel.

vocabulary.note: After a vowel it is 'вчо́ра'. After a consonant and at the start of a sentence, euphony gives 'учо́ра', as it gives 'удо́ма' for 'вдо́ма'. The 'в' of 'вчо́ра' is [w].
Built from 'по́за', beyond, and 'вчо́ра'. Inside the word the 'в' never changes, and it is always [w] before the 'ч'.

example.source: I went to the movies the day before yesterday.

vocabulary.note: With a time word, both in the genitive, it says when: 'мину́лого ти́жня', last week; 'мину́лої субо́ти', last Saturday. The past tense is 'мину́лий час'.

example.source: Olena worked long hours last week.

vocabulary.note: 'Тому́' after a length of time means 'ago', and the length of time is in the accusative: 'ти́ждень тому́', a week ago; 'годи́ну тому́', an hour ago.

example.target: Рік тому́ я не говори́в украї́нською.
example.source: A year ago I didn't speak Ukrainian.
example.source_literal: Year ago I not spoke by-Ukrainian.

vocabulary.source: to go for a walk, to stroll
vocabulary.note: Walking for pleasure, with no destination. The 'л' is soft before 'я'.

example.target: Тара́с і Оле́на гуля́ли в це́нтрі.
example.source: Taras and Olena went for a walk downtown.
example.source_literal: Taras and Olena strolled in center.

vocabulary.note: 'Танцю́ю', 'танцю́єш' in the present, where '-юва-' becomes '-ю-'. The past keeps '-юва-': 'танцюва́в', 'танцюва́ла'.
The same root as 'дзво́ник', bell. The person you phone is in the dative, a case of a later unit, so this unit uses the verb without one.
'Відві́дую', 'відві́дуєш' in the present. The person or place visited is the object, in the accusative: 'відві́дувати бабу́сю', 'відві́дувати музе́й'.

example.target: Мину́лого ро́ку Окса́на ча́сто відві́дувала бабу́сю.
example.source: Last year Oksana often visited her grandmother.
example.source_literal: Of-last of-year Oksana often visited grandmother.

vocabulary.note: 'Запро́шую', 'запро́шуєш' in the present. The person invited is in the accusative, and the event follows 'на' with the accusative: 'запро́шувати дру́га на вечі́рку'.

example.source: Taras is inviting us to a concert.

vocabulary.note: Two or more people meet each other, so the subject is usually plural: 'ми зустріча́лися', 'вони́ зустріча́ються'.
'Чу́ю', 'чу́єш' in the present; past 'чув', 'чу́ла', 'чу́ли'. It names hearing a sound, while 'слу́хати' is listening on purpose.
On foot and in one direction, like 'іти́'. 'Несу́', 'несе́ш' in the present; past 'ніс', 'несла́', 'несло́', 'несли́'.

example.source: Andrii was carrying coffee and tea.

vocabulary.note: A party with friends, usually in the evening; the word comes from 'ве́чір'. The locative is 'на вечі́рці', with 'к' becoming 'ц' before '-і'.

example.source: We were at a party yesterday.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'конце́рту'. You are 'на конце́рті', at a concert, with 'на' as for other events.
It never changes form: 'у кіно́' is both 'at the movies' and 'to the movies'.

example.source: Do you want to go to the movies?

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'фі́льму'. The 'л' is soft before the soft sign.
A public holiday or a family celebration. The locative is 'на свя́ті', at a celebration.

example.source: I read for a long time.

dialogues.title: What did you do on the weekend?
dialogues.context: On Monday morning Oksana and Sam meet at Andrii's café. The two friends say 'ти' to each other; Andrii, who owns the café, says 'ви' to his customers, and they say 'ви' to him. 'На вихідни́х' means 'on the weekend', and 'а по́тім' means 'and then'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Приві́т, Се́ме! Що ти роби́в на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! What did you do on the weekend?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Sam! What you did on weekend?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Приві́т! У субо́ту я відпочива́в. До́вго спав, чита́в, а по́тім гуля́в у па́рку.
lines.source: Hi! On Saturday I relaxed. I slept for a long time, read, and then went for a walk in the park.
lines.source_literal: Hi! In Saturday I rested. Long slept, read, and then strolled in park.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А в неді́лю?
lines.source: And on Sunday?
lines.source_literal: And in Sunday?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У неді́лю я був у кіно́. Фільм був украї́нський і ду́же ціка́вий.
lines.source: On Sunday I went to the movies. The film was Ukrainian and very interesting.
lines.source_literal: In Sunday I was in cinema. Film was Ukrainian and very interesting.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ти до́бре розумі́в?
lines.source: Did you understand it well?
lines.source_literal: You well understood?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тро́хи. Вони́ говори́ли ду́же шви́дко!
lines.source: A little. They spoke very fast!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я в субо́ту була́ на конце́рті.
lines.source: And I went to a concert on Saturday.
lines.source_literal: And I in Saturday was at concert.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: На конце́рті? Хто там співа́в?
lines.source: A concert? Who sang there?
lines.source_literal: At concert? Who there sang?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Співа́ли студе́нти з мого́ університе́ту. Ми до́вго танцюва́ли!
lines.source: Students from my university sang. We danced for a long time!
lines.source_literal: Sang students from my university. We long danced!

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок! Ось ва́ша ка́ва.
lines.source: Good morning! Here is your coffee.
lines.source_literal: Good morning! Here your coffee.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Па́не Андрі́ю, а що ви роби́ли на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Thank you! And what did you do on the weekend, Andrii?
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Mr. Andrii, and what you did on weekend?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Я працюва́в. У ме́не не було́ ча́су відпочива́ти.
lines.source: I worked. I had no time to relax.
lines.source_literal: I worked. At me not was of-time to-rest.

dialogues.title: Yesterday's party
dialogues.context: On Sunday morning Olena drops in on her brother Taras, who did not answer her call the evening before. They say 'ти' to each other. 'До двана́дцятої' means 'until twelve o'clock': it is 'до' with the genitive of 'двана́дцята', with 'годи́на' left out, as in 'о двана́дцятій'.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, я вчо́ра дзвони́ла, а ти не чув!
lines.source: Taras, I called yesterday, and you didn't hear!
lines.source_literal: Taras, I yesterday phoned, and you not heard!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ви́бач, Оле́но. Я був на вечі́рці в кафе́.
lines.source: Sorry, Olena. I was at a party at a café.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: На вечі́рці? І як було́?
lines.source: At a party? And how was it?
lines.source_literal: At party? And how was?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре! Ми співа́ли й танцюва́ли до двана́дцятої.
lines.source: Really good! We sang and danced until twelve.
lines.source_literal: Very well! We sang and danced until twelfth.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Хто співа́в? Ти?
lines.source: Who sang? You?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні, я не співа́в. Співа́ла Со́фія. Вона́ ду́же до́бре співа́є!
lines.source: No, I didn't sing. Sofiia sang. She sings really well!
lines.source_literal: No, I not sang. Sang Sofiia. She very well sings!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А хто танцюва́в?
lines.source: And who danced?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Окса́на, Сем і я. І Андрі́й теж танцюва́в!
lines.source: Oksana, Sam and I. And Andrii danced too!
lines.source_literal: Oksana, Sam and I. And Andrii too danced!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Андрі́й? А що ви ї́ли?
lines.source: Andrii? And what did you eat?
lines.source_literal: Andrii? And what you ate?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Варе́ники й сала́т. А ти що роби́ла вчо́ра?
lines.source: Varenyky and salad. And what did you do yesterday?
lines.source_literal: Varenyky and salad. And you what did yesterday?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Я працюва́ла до деся́тої. По́тім я ду́же хоті́ла спа́ти.
lines.source: I worked until ten. Then I really wanted to sleep.
lines.source_literal: I worked until tenth. Then I very wanted to-sleep.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: У субо́ту в кафе́ бу́де свя́то. Хо́чеш?
lines.source: There will be a celebration at the café on Saturday. Do you want to come?
lines.source_literal: In Saturday in café will-be celebration. You-want?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Так, до́бре!
lines.source: Yes, all right!
lines.source_literal: Yes, well!

dialogues.title: Where were you last week?
dialogues.context: In Iryna Petrivna's Ukrainian class, Oksana is a guest who helps the foreign students practice conversation. Iryna Petrivna says 'ви' to her adult students, and they say 'ви' to her.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́брий день! Се́ме, вас тут не було́ мину́лого ти́жня. Де ви були́?
lines.source: Good afternoon! Sam, you weren't here last week. Where were you?
lines.source_literal: Good day! Sam, of-you here not was of-last of-week. Where you were?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мину́лого ти́жня я був у Льво́ві. Я відві́дував дру́га.
lines.source: Last week I was in Lviv. I was visiting a friend.
lines.source_literal: Of-last of-week I was in Lviv. I visited friend.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У Льво́ві? І що ви там роби́ли?
lines.source: In Lviv? And what did you do there?
lines.source_literal: In Lviv? And what you there did?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ми гуля́ли в це́нтрі й були́ в музе́ї.
lines.source: We walked around downtown and went to a museum.
lines.source_literal: We strolled in center and were in museum.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. А ви, Окса́но? Що ви роби́ли мину́лої субо́ти?
lines.source: Very good. And you, Oksana? What did you do last Saturday?
lines.source_literal: Very well. And you, Oksana? What you did of-last of-Saturday?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я відві́дувала бабу́сю й діду́ся. Вони́ живу́ть дале́ко, і я до́вго ї́хала на авто́бусі.
lines.source: I was visiting my grandmother and grandfather. They live far away, and I was on the bus for a long time.
lines.source_literal: I visited grandmother and grandfather. They live far, and I long rode on bus.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У них було́ свя́то?
lines.source: Did they have a celebration?
lines.source_literal: At them was celebration?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, у діду́ся було́ свя́то. Ми до́вго ї́ли й співа́ли.
lines.source: Yes, Grandpa had a celebration. We ate and sang for a long time.
lines.source_literal: Yes, at grandfather was celebration. We long ate and sang.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ви, Іри́но Петрі́вно? Що ви роби́ли?
lines.source: And you, Iryna Petrivna? What did you do?
lines.source_literal: And you, Iryna Petrivna? What you did?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Я була́ вдо́ма. Я писа́ла нову́ грама́тику.
lines.source: I was at home. I was writing a new grammar book.
lines.source_literal: I was at-home. I wrote new grammar.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Нову́ грама́тику? Для нас?
lines.source: A new grammar book? For us?
lines.source_literal: New grammar? For us?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, для вас. Ось вона́!
lines.source: Yes, for you. Here it is!
lines.source_literal: Yes, for you. Here it!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Яка́ вели́ка кни́га!
lines.source: What a big book!
lines.source_literal: What-kind big book!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: чита́в, ішо́в and йшов, ніс and несла́
grammar.explanation:
Almost every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The past tense brings four points that come up in almost every sentence: the 'в' at the end of a masculine form, two words whose first letter depends on the word before them, the vowel that changes in 'ніс' and 'несла́', and the stress that moves in a few short verbs.

The masculine past of most verbs ends in '-в', and that 'в' always closes the syllable, so it is said [w], as in 'cow', never [v] and never [f]: 'чита́в' [t͡ʃɪˈtɑw], 'був' [buw], 'їв' [jiw]. The same [w] is heard wherever 'в' stands before a consonant: 'вчо́ра' [ˈwt͡ʃɔrɑ], 'позавчо́ра', 'до́вго' [ˈdɔwɦɔ], and 'прокида́вся', where '-ся' follows the 'в'. Before a vowel the letter is [ʋ] again, so the masculine and the feminine of one verb end differently: 'співа́в' ends in [w], while in 'співа́ла' the only 'в' stands before a vowel and is [ʋ].

Euphony, the rule of the unit on stress that makes vowels and consonants alternate from one word to the next, also chooses the first letter of two words in this unit:

- 'учо́ра' and 'вчо́ра' are one word, 'yesterday': 'вчо́ра' after a vowel ('Окса́на вчо́ра співа́ла.'), 'учо́ра' after a consonant and at the start of a sentence ('Сем учо́ра співа́в.', 'Учо́ра йшов дощ.'), as with 'вдо́ма' and 'удо́ма'.
- The past of 'іти́' is 'ішо́в', 'ішла́', 'ішло́', 'ішли́' after a consonant and at the start of a sentence ('Тара́с ішо́в у парк.'), and 'йшов', 'йшла', 'йшло', 'йшли' after a vowel ('Окса́на йшла в парк.'), as with 'іду́' and 'йду'.

With 'й' the word loses a syllable: 'ішо́в' has two syllables and carries the stress mark, while 'йшов' has one and carries none. 'Учо́ра' has three syllables and 'вчо́ра' two, and the stress stays on the 'о'.

A few verbs add the past endings to a stem that ends in a consonant: 'нес-' in 'несла́', 'мог-' in 'могла́'. Their masculine has no '-в': the stem alone ends the word. In the masculine 'ніс' the stem 'нес-' is one closed syllable, so its 'е' becomes 'і', just as 'о' becomes 'і' in 'кіт' against 'кота́' (the unit on nouns). Wherever an ending follows, the syllable is open again and the 'е' returns: 'несла́', 'несло́', 'несли́'. 'Могти́' works the same way: 'міг', 'могла́', 'могли́'. 'Ніс', he carried, is spelled and said like 'ніс', nose, from the first alphabet unit; the sentence shows which one is meant.

Most verbs keep the stress of the infinitive in every past form: 'чита́ти', 'чита́в', 'чита́ла', 'чита́ли'; 'ба́чити', 'ба́чив', 'ба́чила'. A few short verbs stress the last syllable of every past form: 'бу́ти' gives 'був', 'була́', 'було́', 'були́'; 'жи́ти' gives 'жив', 'жила́', 'жили́'; 'пи́ти' gives 'пив', 'пила́', 'пили́'; 'нести́' gives 'ніс', 'несла́'; 'могти́' gives 'міг', 'могла́'; 'іти́' gives 'ішо́в', 'ішла́'. 'Ї́сти' keeps its stress: 'їв', 'ї́ла', 'ї́ли'. Its 'ї' is [ji] in every form, as 'ї' always is, so 'їв' is [jiw]. Learn the stress of these verbs with each form.

The new words follow the familiar rules:

- In 'свя́то' the 'в' follows another consonant of the same root, so no apostrophe is written: the 'я' softens the 'в' slightly and gives [ɑ], with no [j] before it.
- In 'дзвони́ти' the 'дз' is one sound, [d͡z], because it stands inside the root, the same root as 'дзво́ник', bell.
- 'Вечі́рка' comes from 'ве́чір', evening. Its 'і' stays because the syllable 'чір' is closed by the 'р', and the stress moves. Its locative is 'на вечі́рці', with 'к' becoming 'ц' before '-і', as in 'у бібліоте́ці'.
- The 'ц' is hard before 'е' in 'конце́рт' and soft before 'ю' in 'танцюва́ти'.
- 'Фільм' has a soft 'ль' before the 'м', and 'гуля́ти' a soft 'л' before 'я'.
- In the present, '-ува-' becomes '-у-', and '-юва-' becomes '-ю-' ('відві́дую', 'запро́шую', 'танцю́ю'); the past keeps the full suffix, because it is built from the infinitive ('танцюва́в', 'відві́дував', 'запро́шував').

rows: at the end of a word
after a consonant, or first in a sentence
after a consonant, or first in a sentence
after another consonant of the root

examples.source: Taras was walking to the park.
Oksana was walking to the park.
Sam was reading yesterday.
Olena was carrying books.
We were at a celebration.

grammar.title: The past tense: endings for gender and number, not for person
grammar.explanation:
The past tense, 'мину́лий час', says what happened or what was going on before now. Its endings do not show the person, as the endings of the present do: 'я чита́в', 'ти чита́в' and 'він чита́в' use the same word. They show the gender and the number of the subject instead, the way an adjective shows the gender and number of its noun. The form began as a word of that kind: long ago it was used with a form of 'бу́ти', roughly 'I am one-who-has-read', and when 'бу́ти' dropped out of these sentences, the adjective-like word alone became the past tense.

To form the past of almost any verb, take the infinitive, remove '-ти' and add the ending that matches the subject:

- '-в' for a masculine singular subject: 'чита́в', 'говори́в'
- '-ла' for a feminine singular subject: 'чита́ла', 'говори́ла'
- '-ло' for a neuter singular subject: 'чита́ло', 'говори́ло'
- '-ли' for any plural subject: 'чита́ли', 'говори́ли'

The past is built on the infinitive, not on the present, so the changes of the present do not appear in it: 'хо́чу' but 'хоті́в', 'живу́' but 'жив', 'пишу́' but 'писа́в', 'роблю́' but 'роби́в', 'працю́ю' but 'працюва́в'. This makes the past the easiest tense to form. The stress usually stays where the infinitive has it, but a few short verbs move it onto the ending: 'жив', 'жила́', 'жили́'.

The ending follows the subject:

- a masculine noun or 'він': 'Тара́с співа́в.', 'Фільм був ціка́вий.', and also a man's name in '-а', because a man is masculine whatever the ending: 'Мико́ла співа́в.'
- a feminine noun or 'вона́': 'Оле́на працюва́ла.', 'Вечі́рка була́ вели́ка.'
- a neuter noun or 'воно́': 'Свя́то було́ га́рне.'
- a plural noun, 'ми', 'ви' or 'вони́': 'Студе́нти співа́ли.', 'Ми танцюва́ли.'

'Я' and 'ти' have no gender of their own, so the past form shows whether the person is a man or a woman. Sam says 'Я чита́в.' and Oksana says 'Я чита́ла.'; you ask Sam 'Ти чита́в?' and Oksana 'Ти чита́ла?'. 'Ви' takes the plural ending even when it is said to one person, man or woman: 'Іри́но Петрі́вно, ви чита́ли?'. The question words have fixed forms: 'хто' takes the masculine, even when the answer is a woman ('Хто співа́в? Со́фія.'), and 'що' takes the neuter ('Що було́ на вечі́рці?').

Because the form does not show the person, the subject pronoun is usually kept in the past: 'чита́в' alone could mean 'I read', 'you read' or 'he read'. It is left out only when the sentence has just named the subject: 'Я до́вго спав, по́тім чита́в.'

A reflexive verb adds '-ся' after the past ending: 'прокида́вся' for a man, 'прокида́лася' for a woman, 'прокида́лося' for a neuter subject and 'прокида́лися' in the plural. After a vowel, '-ся' also has the shorter form '-сь' of the unit on daily routine ('прокида́лась', 'прокида́лись'); after the 'в' of the masculine only '-ся' is possible.

A few verbs have a past that the rule does not give, or a stress that the infinitive does not show:

- 'бу́ти': 'був', 'була́', 'було́', 'були́'
- 'іти́': 'ішо́в', 'ішла́', 'ішло́', 'ішли́', or 'йшов', 'йшла', 'йшло', 'йшли' after a vowel
- 'могти́': 'міг', 'могла́', 'могло́', 'могли́'
- 'ї́сти': 'їв', 'ї́ла', 'ї́ло', 'ї́ли'
- 'нести́': 'ніс', 'несла́', 'несло́', 'несли́'

'Бу́ти' follows the rule, 'бу-' plus the ending, but moves the stress onto the ending: 'була́', 'було́', 'були́'. 'Могти́' and 'нести́' follow a rule of their own: their past stem ends in a consonant ('мог-', 'нес-'), so the masculine has no '-в' and is the bare stem, with 'і' in its closed syllable. The pasts of 'іти́' and 'ї́сти' are learned as they are.

Every past form in this unit belongs to an imperfective verb. The unit on verbs explained that an imperfective verb presents an action as a process, a habit or a plain fact, so 'Я чита́в' covers what English says with 'I read', 'I was reading', 'I used to read' and 'I have read': 'Ти ба́чив цей фільм?' is 'Have you seen this film?'. The next unit adds perfective verbs, which present one completed action with its result.

examples.source: Taras was reading, and Olena was writing.
Sam, did you dance?
Oksana, did you dance?
Mykola worked for a long time.
We met up at the café.
Who has been eating my cheese?

grammar.title: Був, було́ and не було́: being, having and lacking in the past
grammar.explanation:
In the present a Ukrainian sentence has no word for 'is' ('Тара́с удо́ма.'), and 'є' appears only to say that something exists or that someone has it. In the past every one of these sentences has a form of 'бу́ти', and that form agrees with the subject: 'Тара́с був удо́ма.', 'Оле́на була́ на робо́ті.', 'Ми були́ в кіно́.'

Existence and possession follow the same rule. In 'У ме́не є кіт.' the thing owned, 'кіт', is the subject, and the owner stands after 'у' in the genitive (the unit on family). In the past, 'є' becomes the form of 'бу́ти' that agrees with the thing owned, whoever the owner is:

- 'У ме́не був кіт.' I had a cat; 'кіт' is masculine.
- 'В Окса́ни була́ ку́ртка.' Oksana had a jacket; 'ку́ртка' is feminine.
- 'У нас було́ свя́то.' We had a celebration; 'свя́то' is neuter.
- 'У них були́ гро́ші.' They had money; 'гро́ші' is a plural-only noun.
- 'Тут було́ кафе́.' There was a café here; 'кафе́' is neuter.

The past of 'нема́є' is 'не було́'. The thing that is missing stays in the genitive, so the sentence has no subject, and 'було́' takes the neuter form, the form Ukrainian uses whenever a verb has no subject to agree with. It never changes, whatever the gender or number of the missing thing:

- 'У ме́не нема́є ча́су.' becomes 'У ме́не не було́ ча́су.', I didn't have time.
- 'Тут нема́є кафе́.' becomes 'Тут не було́ кафе́.', there was no café here.
- 'Учо́ра не було́ дощу́.' There was no rain yesterday; the genitive of 'дощ' is 'дощу́', with the stress on the ending.

The same pattern says that a person was not somewhere: 'Андрі́я не було́ вдо́ма.', literally 'of-Andrii not was at-home', means 'Andrii wasn't at home.' The pronouns take their genitive forms, which are spelled like the accusative forms of the unit on food and drink: 'мене́', 'тебе́', 'його́', 'її́', 'нас', 'вас', 'їх'. 'Мене́ не було́ на вечі́рці.' is 'I wasn't at the party.' After a preposition the genitive of 'я' is stressed 'ме́не', as in 'у ме́не'. Both 'Андрі́й не був удо́ма.' and 'Андрі́я не було́ вдо́ма.' are correct; the second, with the genitive, is the usual way to say that someone was absent.

Predicative words, which form the whole predicate of a sentence with no subject (the unit on weather), take 'було́' in the past and 'бу́де' in the future, neuter again because there is no subject:

- 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.' It is cold today.
- 'Учо́ра було́ хо́лодно.' It was cold yesterday.
- 'За́втра бу́де хо́лодно.' It will be cold tomorrow.

The question 'Як було́?', how was it?, is built the same way, with no subject.

Rain and snow that 'go' take the past of 'іти́', which agrees with 'дощ' or 'сніг', the subject: 'Іде́ дощ.' becomes 'Ішо́в дощ.', or 'Учо́ра йшов дощ.' after a vowel; 'Іде́ сніг.' becomes 'Ішо́в сніг.'

examples.source: Taras had a party.

examples.target: Тут було́ кафе́, а за́раз тут банк.
examples.source: There used to be a café here, and now there's a bank.
examples.source_literal: Here was café, and now here bank.

examples.source: I wasn't at home.

examples.target: Сього́дні те́пло, а вчо́ра було́ хо́лодно.
examples.source: It's warm today, but yesterday it was cold.
examples.source_literal: Today warm, and yesterday was cold.

examples.source: It was snowing.

grammar.title: When it happened: вчо́ра, мину́лого ти́жня, рік тому́
grammar.explanation:
A sentence in the past usually says when, and Ukrainian has three ways to do it, each built from things you already know: an adverb, a noun phrase in the genitive, and a length of time with 'тому́'.

The adverbs answer 'коли́?' by themselves: 'вчо́ра' (or 'учо́ра', by euphony), 'позавчо́ра', and 'сього́дні', which works for the past too ('Сього́дні я до́вго спав.'). They combine with the words for parts of the day: 'учо́ра вра́нці', yesterday morning.

A noun phrase with 'мину́лий', past or last, names the week, the year or the day, in the genitive and with no preposition: 'мину́лого ти́жня', last week; 'мину́лого ро́ку', last year (the genitive of 'рік' is 'ро́ку'); 'мину́лої субо́ти', last Saturday; 'мину́лої неді́лі', last Sunday. This is a new job for the genitive, called the genitive of time: it names the time at which something happened. A day can also take 'у' with the accusative, as in the unit on weather: 'у субо́ту', and with 'мину́лий', 'у мину́лу субо́ту'. In a sentence about the past, 'у субо́ту' alone means last Saturday.

'Тому́' after a length of time means 'ago'. The length of time is in the accusative, so a masculine noun does not change and a feminine noun in '-а' takes '-у':

- 'рік тому́', a year ago
- 'ти́ждень тому́', a week ago
- 'годи́ну тому́', an hour ago
- 'хвили́ну тому́', a minute ago
- 'два ро́ки тому́', two years ago, with the number and the noun as the unit on numbers taught

'Тому́' always comes after the length of time. It is a different word from 'тому́', so or therefore, of the A1 consolidation unit: the two are adverbs with one spelling, and their position tells them apart, since 'тому́' meaning therefore begins its clause.

Words of frequency and duration describe habits and long activities in the past, which is why they go with the imperfective verbs of this unit: 'Мину́лого ро́ку я ча́сто гуля́в у па́рку.', 'Ми до́вго танцюва́ли.' With the double negative of the unit on daily routine, 'Я ніко́ли не танцюва́в.' means 'I have never danced.'

The questions about the past use the same words: 'Коли́ ти був у Льво́ві?', 'Що ти роби́в на вихідни́х?', 'Де ви були́ мину́лого ти́жня?'. In the answer the time marker usually comes first, or straight after the subject, and the new information comes last, as is usual in Ukrainian. 'Учо́ра я був у кіно́.' tells where I was yesterday; 'У кіно́ я був учо́ра.' tells when I was at the movies. In 'був учо́ра' the word follows the consonant 'в', so euphony gives 'учо́ра'.

rows: adverb; учо́ра after a consonant or at the start

examples.target: Мину́лого ро́ку я ча́сто гуля́в у па́рку.
examples.source: Last year I often went for walks in the park.
examples.source_literal: Of-last of-year I often strolled in park.

examples.target: Два ро́ки тому́ Сем жив у Кана́ді.
examples.source: Two years ago Sam lived in Canada.
Taras was here an hour ago.

examples.target: У мину́лу субо́ту ми були́ в кіно́.
examples.source: Last Saturday we went to the movies.
examples.source_literal: In last Saturday we were in cinema.

examples.source: When were you in Lviv?
It was yesterday that I went to the movies.

culture.title: Weekends, celebrations and songs
culture.text:
Saturday and Sunday are 'вихідні́', the days off, and many people spend them away from home. In the cities people go for walks in parks and along rivers, meet friends in cafés, and go to concerts, the theater and the cinema. Walking with no destination, 'гуля́ти', is a favorite way to spend a free evening. On Monday a colleague is likely to ask 'Що ти роби́в на вихідни́х?', or, to a woman, 'Що ти роби́ла на вихідни́х?': What did you do on the weekend?

Singing together is an old and living part of Ukrainian celebrations. At family celebrations such as birthdays and weddings, guests often sing folk songs at the table, and many people know the words of dozens of them. The winter holidays have songs of their own:

- 'коля́дки' are sung at Christmas by groups of singers who go from house to house
- 'щедрі́вки' are sung around the New Year and wish the household a rich year

The best known of them, 'Щедри́к', arranged by the composer Mykola Leontovych, became known in English as 'Carol of the Bells'. In the Ukrainian words a swallow flies to the house and sings that the family will have a good year.

In villages, young people used to spend winter evenings at 'вечорни́ці', gatherings with songs, dances, games and work such as spinning. The word shares its root with 'ве́чір' and 'вечі́рка', and today's party in a café is its city descendant.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its English meaning
Match each time expression with its English meaning

choices: Sam danced in the park yesterday.
Sam sang in the park yesterday.
Sam went for a walk in the park yesterday.

exercises.prompt: Which past ending goes with the subject 'вона́'?
exercises.explanation: The past ending shows the gender and number of the subject: '-в' masculine, '-ла' feminine, '-ло' neuter, '-ли' plural. 'Вона́ чита́ла.'

exercises.prompt: Oksana says 'I was reading.' Which sentence does she use?
exercises.explanation: 'Я' has no gender of its own, so the past form shows the speaker's: a woman says 'Я чита́ла.' and a man says 'Я чита́в.' The ending '-ли' is the plural.
'Оле́на' is feminine, so the past of 'бу́ти' is 'була́', with the stress on the ending.

exercises.hint_source: Mykola danced for a long time.
exercises.explanation: Mykola is a man, so the masculine '-в' is used, although his name ends in '-а'. The past keeps the '-юва-' of the infinitive: 'танцюва́в'.

exercises.prompt: How is the 'в' at the end of 'чита́в' said?
choices: [w], as in 'cow', because it closes the syllable
exercises.explanation: A 'в' that closes a syllable, at the end of a word or before a consonant, is [w]: [t͡ʃɪˈtɑw]. Ukrainian 'в' never turns into [f].
'Ді́ти' is plural, so the ending is '-ли', as in 'танцюва́ли'. 'Й' follows because 'співа́ли' ends in a vowel.

exercises.prompt: Sam asks his teacher, whom he calls 'ви': 'Іри́но Петрі́вно, ви ___ вдо́ма?' Which form fills the gap?
exercises.explanation: 'Ви' always takes the plural past, even when it is said to one woman: 'ви були́'.
The past of 'ї́сти' is 'їв', 'ї́ла', 'ї́ло', 'ї́ли'. 'Сем' is masculine, so the form is 'їв', said [jiw].
'Могти́' has the stem 'мог-'. The feminine adds '-ла' to it: 'могла́'. Only the masculine 'міг' changes its vowel.

exercises.prompt: What is the past of 'нести́' with 'він'?
exercises.explanation: The stem 'нес-' ends in a consonant, so the masculine has no '-в'; in its closed syllable 'е' becomes 'і': 'ніс'. 'Несла́' is the feminine and 'несли́' the plural.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Окса́на ___ в парк.', 'Oksana was walking to the park'?
exercises.explanation: After a vowel, euphony turns the 'і' of 'ішла́' into 'й': 'Окса́на йшла'. 'Йшов' is the masculine.

exercises.prompt_target: Мину́лого ти́жня я завжди́ ___ о сьо́мій.
exercises.hint_source: Oksana says: Last week I always woke up at seven.
exercises.explanation: The speaker is a woman, so the ending is '-ла', and the reflexive '-ся' follows it: 'прокида́лася', or 'прокида́лась' with the shorter form after a vowel.
The thing owned is the subject, so the verb agrees with 'свя́то', a neuter noun: 'було́'. Taras, the owner, is in the genitive after 'у'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'В Окса́ни був кіт', with the masculine 'був', although Oksana is a woman?
choices: The past of 'бу́ти' is always masculine
'Кіт' is the subject and it is masculine; Oksana, the owner, is in the genitive after 'у'
'В Окса́ни' is masculine because it ends in '-и'
exercises.explanation: In a sentence of possession the thing owned is the subject, and the verb agrees with it. 'В Окса́ни була́ ку́ртка.' has 'була́' because 'ку́ртка' is feminine.

exercises.prompt: In 'Оле́ни не було́ на вечі́рці.', why is 'Оле́ни' in the genitive?
choices: Olena is the owner of the party
After 'не було́', the person or thing that is absent is in the genitive
exercises.explanation: 'Не було́' is the past of 'нема́є' and takes the genitive of whoever or whatever was absent. The sentence has no subject, so 'було́' is neuter: 'Olena wasn't at the party.'

exercises.hint_source: It was cold the day before yesterday.
exercises.explanation: 'Хо́лодно' is a predicative word in a sentence with no subject, so the past of 'бу́ти' is the neuter 'було́'.

exercises.prompt: Two women sang at the party. How do you ask 'Who sang?'
exercises.explanation: 'Хто' always takes the masculine singular, whoever the answer turns out to be.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'a year ago'?
exercises.explanation: 'Тому́' meaning 'ago' follows the length of time: 'рік тому́'. 'Мину́лого ро́ку' means 'last year'.

exercises.prompt: In 'мину́лої субо́ти', which case are the two words in, and why?
choices: The genitive: with no preposition, it names the time when something happened
The accusative, because it follows a verb
exercises.explanation: This is the genitive of time: 'мину́лого ти́жня', 'мину́лого ро́ку', 'мину́лої субо́ти'. With 'у' a day is in the accusative instead: 'у мину́лу субо́ту'.

exercises.prompt: At the café on Monday, what does Sam say he did on Sunday?
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'У неді́лю я був у кіно́.' It was Oksana who went to a concert, and Andrii who worked.

exercises.prompt: In the conversation about the party, who sang?
exercises.explanation: Taras says 'Ні, я не співа́в. Співа́ла Со́фія.' Oksana, Sam, Taras and Andrii danced.

exercises.prompt: In Iryna Petrivna's class, what does Sam say he did last week?
choices: He was in Lviv, visiting a friend.
He was at home, writing a grammar book.
He was at his grandfather's celebration.
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'Мину́лого ти́жня я був у Льво́ві. Я відві́дував дру́га.' Iryna Petrivna was at home, and Oksana visited her grandparents.

exercises.prompt_source: What did you do yesterday, Sam?

exercises.hint_source: We walked in the park for a long time.

exercises.prompt_source: Sam says: I was at a party yesterday.
exercises.explanation: Sam is a man, so the form is 'був'. 'Учо́ра' begins a sentence or follows a consonant, and 'вчо́ра' follows a vowel.
'Те́пло' is a predicative word with no subject, so 'бу́ти' takes the neuter 'було́'.
The usual way to say that someone was absent is 'не було́' with the genitive: 'Тара́са не було́'. 'Тара́с не був' is also correct.

exercises.prompt_source: Iryna Petrivna, where were you last week?
answers: Іри́но Петрі́вно, де ви були́ мину́лого ти́жня?
Де ви були́ мину́лого ти́жня, Іри́но Петрі́вно?
exercises.explanation: The name is in the vocative, 'ви' takes the plural 'були́' even for one person, and 'last week' is the genitive of time 'мину́лого ти́жня'.
